On 20 May 1498 the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama arrived at Calicut (Kozhikode) on the Malabar coast of India. It was the first voyage from Europe to India by sea, and it opened a direct ocean route between Europe and Asia.

Da Gama left Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships. He followed the route that Bartolomeu Dias had opened round the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, then sailed up the east coast of Africa. At Malindi, in today's Kenya, he took on an experienced Indian Ocean pilot, who guided him across the open sea to India in under a month.

Calicut was the main pepper port of the Malabar coast, ruled by a king known as the Zamorin and full of Arab, Persian and Gujarati merchants. The Portuguese gifts looked poor to the Zamorin, and the Muslim traders saw them as rivals. Relations soured, and da Gama left in August with a modest load of spices. The voyage home was hard; many of his men died of scurvy. Still, the cargo sold for a large profit.

The consequences were huge:

  • Portugal sent fleets every year. One, under Cabral in 1500, touched Brazil on the way.
  • Da Gama's second voyage, in 1502, was marked by great violence against Muslim shipping.
  • The Portuguese seized Goa in 1510 and Malacca in 1511, and tried to control the spice trade with forts and naval patrols.
  • Spices could now bypass the old route through Mamluk Egypt and Venice.
sum: On 20 May 1498 the Portuguese captain Vasco da Gama arrived at Calicut (Kozhikode) on the Malabar coast of India. It was the first voyage from Europe to India by sea, and it opened a direct ocean route between Europe and Asia.
